job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Colin Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings I'm at the back-bedroom desk in my dad's terraced house in Eastfield, with my gran's radio coming through the wall. I finished a finance degree with a good result and did ten weeks at Pennywise Labs, a tiny payments start-up, where I built spreadsheets. Now I send applications with an AI helper doing my first drafts, then I do bookkeeping for a barber and a bakery for about ninety pounds a week. Evenings I teach myself bits of Python, because why not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, nobody has to panic. I use these tools every day, so I'd tell friends they're useful but they're not magic. Online I'd probably post a joke about the hype, since the hype is half the entertainment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, a flat world is still a hard world for me. Entry finance jobs near Eastfield are rare, and my loan is bigger than a car. The barber and the bakery pay cash, but ninety pounds a week doesn't cover the repayments plus my share of the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep pushing applications, a handful a day, and aim some at jobs that mention data or automation, since I can already do that. I'd try to add three more small bookkeeping clients and charge a bit more. Every Sunday I'd spend two hours on a small project I can show, like a cash-flow dashboard for the bakery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Restless, to be honest. Not terrified, because I can feel myself doing something, but I get impatient with the pace. My dad says I'm too hard on myself and my gran says I should eat more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a cash-flow dashboard for the bakery, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's real. The baker, Mrs Okafor, currently tracks everything in a notebook, and I can build her a simple view that tells her when she's short before payday. If it works, that's a case study I can show an employer, and she'll tell her friends who run shops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the repayments if the new clients don't appear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I ask for the payment break the loan company offers and pay more interest later. I hate that choice, but I'd rather do that than skip food. I've already read the terms, and I know which form to fill in.

say: I'd say nobody needs to panic: the tools are **useful**, not magic.
Online I'd post a **joke** about the hype.
think: A flat world is still **hard**: few entry jobs nearby and a loan bigger than a car.
Ninety pounds a week doesn't cover **repayments** plus bills.
do: Send a handful of **applications** a day, some aimed at data and automation roles.
Build a cash-flow **dashboard** for the bakery on Sundays.
feel: **Restless** and impatient, but not terrified, because he is doing something.
S0.quote: The barber and the bakery pay cash, but ninety pounds a week doesn't cover the repayments plus my share of the bills.
fieldNote: Adaptive in practice: he builds proof of skill with real clients.
Debt and few local openings keep him **anxious** even when nothing changes.
Already knows the loan's payment-break form, so he plans for the worst without drama.

steps.text: Send five applications a day, aiming at data and automation roles
Add three more small bookkeeping clients and raise the price
Build a cash-flow dashboard for the bakery as a case study
Ask the loan company for a payment break if clients don't appear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and people should get ready, not hide. I'd tell my mates to learn the tools now, because they're already making some entry tasks disappear. And I'd say the people who gain most should share the gains, so I'd back stronger unions and some regulation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my kind of job is right in the firing line. Reconciliations, invoice checks and reports are the first things software takes, and at Pennywise Labs I watched a script replace what a junior would do. That's the bad news, but the good news is I'm already using this stuff daily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go hard on the tools: build small automations for my bookkeeping clients and show them to employers. I'd apply to roles titled analyst, operations or finance technology. And I'd join a union for young professionals, because individuals negotiate badly when firms hold all the cards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and nervous in equal parts. It's like standing at the top of a slide, and I'd rather go down than stay frozen. The nervous part is the debt, which doesn't care if I'm clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the gains should be shared. What would sharing look like in your own life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Practically, a firm that automates the junior team should pay into retraining and take on graduates anyway. In my own bookkeeping, I charge the bakery less because the software does half the work, and I'd rather keep her trust than the extra money. I think small fairness adds up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop you from getting ahead of the curve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, really. Courses and certificates cost, and an unpaid trial week is hard when I'm paying a loan. If nothing else, I can keep my costs low at home with my dad and gran, which is the one cushion I do have.

say: I'd tell mates to **learn the tools** now, not hide from them.
I'd back **unions** and regulation so gains are shared.
think: My kind of job is in the **firing line**: reconciliations and invoice checks go first.
The good news is I'm already using **AI** every day.
do: Build small **automations** for my bookkeeping clients and show employers.
Apply for **analyst**, operations and finance technology roles.
feel: **Excited** and nervous, like the top of a slide, with debt that ignores cleverness.
S1.quote: The nervous part is the debt, which doesn't care if I'm clever.
fieldNote: Moves toward change early and sees AI as a tool he can use.
His left-leaning view shows in wanting **shared gains** and stronger unions.
Names money, not skill, as his main limit.

steps.text: Build small automations for the barber's and bakery's books
Apply for analyst, operations and finance technology roles
Join a union for young professionals
Keep living at home to hold costs low

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the biggest thing that will happen in our lives and we're unprepared. Publicly I'd push for a basic income, public ownership of the biggest models, and training paid by the companies. I'd say it loudly and keep saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think most of what a finance graduate does goes in two years, and I'd be competing with software at nothing a day. The debt makes it worse, since a loan doesn't cancel because the job did. I also think a few people get very rich, and I'm not one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put every spare penny against the loan and try to turn bookkeeping into something real, like a small service for shops using AI to do the grunt work. I'd get as many clients as I can before everyone does the same. I'd also get active in groups pushing for basic income, because I can't solve this alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dizzy. It's a mix of thrill and dread, because it's the future I read about, only now with my name in it. I'd lie awake doing sums on the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the loan doesn't cancel. What would you want done about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If machines do the thinking work and graduates can't earn, student loans should pause or shrink, at least for people out of work. I'd be first in the queue for that. Otherwise a whole generation pays for a promise the economy broke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots for hands-on work come around 2031. Does that change your bookkeeping plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, since mine is thinking work and goes first, but it shows there's no hiding in physical jobs either. So my bridge is only a few years. That's why I'd rush to build clients and savings fast, and be loud about the policy.

say: I'd push for a **basic income** and training paid by the companies.
I'd say it **loudly** and keep saying it.
think: Most of what a finance graduate does goes in **two years**.
A **loan** doesn't cancel because the job did.
do: Put every spare penny against the **loan**.
Sign up as many **bookkeeping clients** as I can before everyone does the same.
feel: **Dizzy**, with thrill and dread: the future he read about, with his name in it.
S2.quote: If machines do the thinking work and graduates can't earn, student loans should pause or shrink, at least for people out of work.
fieldNote: Sees the speed clearly and expects his own entry route to disappear.
Takes political action seriously, because he knows he **cannot solve it alone**.
Quick plan, but nothing he can use to pay down debt this year.

steps.text: Sign up as many small bookkeeping clients as possible within six months
Put every spare pound against the student loan
Join a campaign for basic income and paused loan payments
Use AI to do the grunt work in client books

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a window, and I'd tell people to use it. I'd say start now: learn the tools, build a small business, and push for rules and retraining in parallel. I'd keep my tone upbeat but serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I can make this work if I'm quick. In five years I could have a real client base, paid off a lot of the loan and learned enough to jump to whatever the next thing is. The risk is that everyone has the same idea, and the market for little AI bookkeepers fills up fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any entry job in a finance team that lets me learn their systems, while keeping my own clients. I'd build one thing a year, like a dashboard or an automation, and put it in a portfolio. And I'd save four hundred a month towards a cushion and a possible move to the bigger city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Optimistic but wary. I'd say about seven out of ten hopeful. The remaining three are for the debt and the chance that I'm underestimating how fast this goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does moving to the bigger city add that Eastfield doesn't have?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jobs, mostly. There are about forty finance and operations employers there versus maybe five here, and meetups where people actually hire. I'd leave Dad and Gran, which I'd hate, but I'd come home at weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do about the crowded market of little AI bookkeepers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd focus on trust, a specific kind of shop, and my own face on the service. Software is cheap, but a person who explains the numbers over a coffee is harder to copy. I'd go deep with a few trades like barbers and bakers rather than wide.

say: I'd tell people to **start now**: learn tools, build something, push for rules.
I'd keep my tone **upbeat** but serious.
think: I can make this work **if I'm quick**: clients, less debt, skills.
The risk is that **everyone** has the same idea.
do: Take any entry job in a **finance team** while keeping my clients.
Build **one project** a year for a portfolio.
Save **four hundred** a month towards a cushion and a move.
feel: **Optimistic but wary**: about seven out of ten hopeful.
S3.quote: Software is cheap, but a person who explains the numbers over a coffee is harder to copy.
fieldNote: Five years gives him a plan with a **portfolio** and a possible move.

steps.text: Take an entry job in a finance team and keep the side clients
Build one portfolio project a year, like a dashboard
Save four hundred a month for a cushion
Plan a move to the bigger city within two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is time to do this well. I'd say schools and universities need to change what they teach, and employers should rebuild graduate schemes around people working with AI. I'd also tell people not to wait for permission.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel okay. In ten years I could be a decent analyst or run a small firm, with my loan gone. Somewhere in those years I'd probably be rebuilding my job several times, and honestly that sounds more interesting than scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a job as soon as one comes, keep growing my own clients, and take one new skill a year, maybe data engineering one year and a financial regulation course the next. I'd build a little savings pot and maybe buy a small flat before prices change. And I'd vote for rules that make companies share the gains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly, with a bit of impatience. It's like having a long runway and still wanting to take off now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the first year of that look like in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, get my cash flow steady: one proper job, one more client, and a monthly budget I actually follow. Then a short evening course every few months. I wouldn't try to do everything in the first year, because burning out is the real risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change what you tell your friends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd tell my friends that nobody has to rush into another degree out of fear. Pick one useful skill, work on real things, and keep a list of what you've built. It's the lists that get you hired, not the stress.

say: I'd say schools and employers should **rebuild** what graduates learn.
I'd tell people **not to wait** for permission.
think: I feel **okay**: ten years could mean an analyst role or a small firm, with no loan.
Rebuilding my job several times sounds more **interesting** than scary.
do: Take the first proper **job** and add one more client.
Build a **savings pot** and consider a small flat.
feel: **Calm**, mostly, with a bit of impatience on a long runway.
S4.quote: Pick one useful skill, work on real things, and keep a list of what you've built.
fieldNote: With a decade, he views change as **interesting** rather than a threat.
Knows burnout is his real risk, so he paces himself.
Advice to friends comes from his own bookkeeping clients.

steps.text: Take the first proper finance job and add one more client
Learn one new skill a year through short evening courses
Build a savings pot toward a small flat
Vote for rules that make companies share the gains

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question, because two years isn't enough to pay down a loan or build real clients. What would help is paused loan payments for people out of work, a public training fund, and employers who keep hiring graduates even when software can do the junior tasks.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that being adaptable isn't the same as being safe. I'm quick with the tools and I'm still anxious, because the pay doesn't follow the skill.

headlineQuote: Being adaptable isn't the same as being safe. I'm quick with the tools and I'm still anxious, because the pay doesn't follow the skill.
portrait: Colin, 23, has a **good finance degree** and a big loan, and lives with his dad and gran.
He uses AI **every day**, writes applications with it and automates bookkeeping for a barber and a bakery.
He wants unions, regulation and **shared gains**, and would back paused loan payments for people out of work.
His mood stays **anxious** in the first scenarios because debt and few local jobs outweigh his skills.
With five or ten years he becomes **uneasy** rather than alarmed, since he can build clients and a portfolio.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries him most: two years won't pay down a loan or build real clients.
whatWouldHelp: **Paused loan payments** for people out of work, a public training fund, and employers who keep hiring graduates.
